en: Thus have I heard: [Majjhima Nikāya 76, the Sandaka Sutta]
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Now at that time the wanderer Sandaka was residing in the Pilakkha Cave together with a large assembly of wanderers, numbering about five hundred.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Ānanda emerged from seclusion and addressed the bhikkhus:
“Come, friends, let us go to the Devakata pond to see the cave.
“Very well, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with many bhikkhus, went to the Devakata pond.

Now at that time, the wanderer Sandaka was seated together with a large assembly of wanderers who were making a great clamor and loud noise, engaged in various kinds of worldly talk, such as: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers,
talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drinks,
talk of clothes, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of perfumes, talk of kinsmen, and talk of vehicles.
Talk about villages, talk about market towns, talk about cities, talk about the countryside, talk about women, talk about heroes,

talk about streets, talk about wells, talk about departed ancestors, talk about various matters, talk about speculations concerning the world, talk about speculations concerning the ocean, or talk about "thus it was" and "thus it will be.
Then the wanderer Sandaka saw the Venerable Ānanda coming from afar.
Having seen them, he quieted his own assembly:
"Sirs, be silent; do not make a noise.
This disciple of the ascetic Gotama is coming—the ascetic Ānanda."
"Furthermore, among the disciples of the ascetic Gotama who reside in Kosambī, this ascetic Ānanda is one of them.
Those venerable ones desire little noise, are trained in little noise, and speak in praise of little noise;
perhaps, having perceived that the assembly is quiet, he might think it appropriate to approach."
Then those wanderers became silent.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the wanderer Sandaka.
Then the wanderer Sandaka said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, venerable Ānanda; welcome to the venerable Ānanda.
It has been a long time since the venerable Ānanda made the occasion to come here.
Let the venerable Ānanda sit down; this seat is prepared.”
The Venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat.
The wanderer Sandaka also took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As the wanderer Sandaka was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to him:
“Sandaka, for what discussion are you sitting together here now, and what was your conversation that was left unfinished?
“Let be, Master Ānanda, this discussion for which we are sitting together here now.
That discussion will not be difficult for Master Ānanda to hear later on as well.”
“It would be well if the venerable Ānanda himself were to deliver a discourse on the Dhamma concerning his own teacher’s doctrine.
“In that case, Sandaka, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, sir,” the wanderer Sandaka replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda said this: "Sandaka,
these four ways of living that are not the holy life have been declared by that Blessed One— the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
and four kinds of holy lives that do not provide consolation have also been declared, wherein a wise person would not, even with effort, find satisfaction."
“One might not live the holy life, or if one does live it, one might not attain the true Dhamma that is wholesome. “But which, Master Ānanda,

are those four ways of living the non-holy life that have been declared by the Blessed One— the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One— wherein a wise person would not, even with effort, live the holy life?”
“Would he dwell, and while dwelling, would he not master the method, the Dhamma, and what is wholesome?
“In this case, Sandaka, a certain teacher holds such a doctrine and such a view:
‘There is no giving, there is no sacrifice, there is no offering; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done.’”
There is no result of kamma; there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father;

there are no beings who arise spontaneously; and there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have attained the right path and practiced rightly, who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make them known.
When this person, composed of the four great elements, passes away, earth returns to and merges with the body of earth;
water returns to and merges with the body of water; fire returns to and merges with the body of fire; wind returns to and merges with the body of wind;
and space takes over the sense faculties.
Carrying the dead man with a chair as the fifth, the men go forth;
their footprints remain visible only as far as the cremation ground.
The bones turn the color of pigeon droppings.
Sacrifices end in talk;
what is called "giving" is merely a conventional designation for what has been given.
Those who speak of there being something [substantial] are empty, false prattlers.
‘Both the fool and the wise, with the breakup of the body, are annihilated and destroyed; they do not exist after death.
In this regard, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus:
‘This venerable teacher speaks thus and holds such a view:’...

There is no giving, there is no sacrifice, there is no offering; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done; there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father;

there are no beings who arise spontaneously; there are in the world no recluses or brahmins who have attained rightly and practiced rightly, who have themselves realized this world and the other world by direct knowledge.
Having realized the world for themselves through direct higher knowledge, they proclaim it.

This person consists of the four great elements; when he dies, earth returns to the earth-element and passes away into it, water returns to the water-element and passes away into it, fire returns to the fire-element and passes away into it, and wind returns to the wind-element.
It departs and does not follow; the sense-faculties pass away into space.
Men carry the dead on a litter as the fifth person; their footprints are seen only as far as the cremation ground.
The bones turn the color of pigeon-droppings.
Sacrifices end in talk;
giving is merely what has been ordained for the purpose of giving.
Those who speak of there being something [substantial] are empty and false prattlers.
‘Both the fool and the wise, with the breakup of the body, are annihilated, perish, and do not exist after death.
If this teacher’s word is true, then what I have not done here has been done by me, and what I have not lived out here has been lived out by me.

We are both exactly equal in this matter, having attained the same state as one who does not say: ‘Both, with the breakup of the body, shall be annihilated, shall perish, and shall not exist after death.’”
Moreover, this nakedness, shaven head, crouching exertion, and plucking out of hair and beard of our venerable teacher is excessive;
for while I dwell in a bed crowded with children, enjoy Kāsī sandalwood, wear garlands, scents, and unguents,
and accept gold and silver, I shall— by means of this venerable teacher— attain an identical destination in the life hereafter.
Knowing what and seeing what would I practice the holy life under this teacher?
Having understood, "This is an abode of the unholy life," he becomes disillusioned with that holy life and departs.
This, Sandaka, is the first dwelling in the holy life declared by that Blessed One— who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
in which a wise person would not live the holy life with its essentials, nor, while living it,
would succeed in attaining the methodical Dhamma that is wholesome.
Furthermore, Sandaka, here a certain teacher holds such a doctrine and such a view:
‘One who acts, one who causes to act; one who cuts, one who causes to cut; one who cooks, one who causes to cook; one who grieves, one who causes to grieve;
one who tires, one who causes to tire; one who trembles, one who causes to tremble; one who takes life, one who takes what is not given, one who breaks into a dwelling... [and so forth].
For one who robs by stealth, who commits burglary, who stands as a highwayman, who goes to another's wife, or who speaks falsehood— no evil is done. Even if, with a razor-edged wheel,
one were to make a single meat-mound, a single mass of flesh, of all the living beings on this earth, there would be no evil on that account, nor any arrival of evil.

‘If one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and causing to kill, mutilating and causing to mutilate, torturing and causing to torture, there would be no evil on that account, nor would there be any arrival of evil.

And if one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there would be no merit on that account, nor would there be any arrival of merit.
There is no merit, there is no arrival of merit, from giving, self-control, restraint, or truthful speech.’”
In this regard, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus:
‘This venerable teacher speaks thus and holds such a view:
“For one who acts or causes to act, who cuts or causes to cut, who cooks or causes to cook, who grieves or causes to grieve, who exerts himself or causes to exert himself...”’
For one who causes exhaustion, who trembles, who causes others to tremble, who takes life, who takes what is not given, who breaks into dwellings,
who carries off plunder, who commits robbery, who stands as a highwayman, who goes to another’s wife,
or who speaks falsehood— no evil is done. Even if, with a razor-edged wheel, one were to [sweep] the living beings on this earth...
One might make a single heap of flesh, a mass of flesh; there is no evil on that account, no arrival of evil.

Even if one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and causing to kill, mutilating and causing to mutilate, cooking and causing to cook, there is no evil on that account, no arrival of evil.
Even if one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there is no merit on that account, no arrival of merit.
"There is no merit in giving, self-control, restraint, or speaking the truth; there is no arrival of merit.
If this is the true word of that venerable teacher, then what has been done by me here has not been done, and what has been lived by me here has not been lived.
We two are here exactly equal, having attained the same state as an ascetic—even though I do not say, "Of the two of us acting, no evil is committed."
Moreover, this nakedness, shaven head, crouching exertion, and plucking out of hair and beard of our venerable teacher are excessive;
for while I dwell in a bed crowded with children, enjoy Kāsi sandalwood, wear garlands, scents, and unguents,
and accept gold and silver, I shall have the same destination as this venerable teacher in the life hereafter.
Knowing what and seeing what should I practice the holy life under this Teacher?
Realizing, "This is an abode of the unholy life," he becomes disillusioned with that holy life and departs.
This, Sandaka, is the second way of living the spiritual life that has been declared by that Blessed One— the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
in which a wise person would not live the spiritual life with confidence,
and while living there, would not achieve the method, the Dhamma, and what is wholesome.
Furthermore, Sandaka, here a certain teacher holds such a doctrine and such a view:
"There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings;
beings are defiled without cause and without condition."
There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings;
beings are purified without cause and without condition.
There is no power, no energy, no human strength, and no human exertion.

‘All beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are powerless, devoid of strength, devoid of vigor, subject to the transformation of destiny, chance, and inherent nature, and they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth.
In this regard, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus:
‘This venerable teacher speaks in such a way and holds such a view:’...
There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause and without condition.
There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause and without condition.
There is no power, no energy, no human strength, no human exertion; all beings...
‘All breathing things, all beings, all souls, the powerless, the helpless, and devoid of energy, are transformed by destiny, chance, and inherent nature,
and experience pleasure and pain within the six classes of birth.
If this teacher’s word is true, then what was left undone by me here has been done, and what was unaccomplished by me here has been accomplished.”
In this matter, we two are exactly equal and have attained the same state of recluseship; yet I do not say that "we both shall be purified without cause and without condition.

However, the nakedness, the shaving of the head, the exertion in the squatting posture, and the plucking out of hair and beard of this venerable teacher are superfluous, compared to me who, dwelling in a bed crowded with children, enjoying Kāsī sandalwood, and using garlands, perfumes, and ointments...
"By accepting gold and silver and possessing them, I shall have an identical destination in the future life as this venerable teacher.
Knowing what and seeing what, then, would I lead the holy life under this teacher?
[I would realize: 'This is an unchaste way of living.'"
Having understood this, one becomes disillusioned with that holy life and departs from it. This, Sandaka,
is the third kind of dwelling in a life that is not the true holy life, as declared by the Blessed One— the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
in which a wise person would not dwell in the holy life even for a moment.
And Vāsava would not attain the method, the Dhamma that is wholesome.
Furthermore, Sandaka, here some teacher holds such a doctrine and such a view:
"These seven bodies are unmade, not made by any maker, uncreated, not created by a creator, barren, fixed like a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar."
They do not move, they do not change, they do not obstruct one another, and they are not capable of bringing about pleasure, pain, or both pleasure and pain for one another.
Which seven?
The earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, pleasure, pain, and the living being as the seventh.
These seven bodies are unmade, not fashioned by a maker, uncreated, not brought into being by a creator, barren, fixed like a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar.
They do not move, they do not change, and they do not obstruct one another. They are incapable of bringing about pleasure, pain, or both pleasure and pain for one another.
In this regard, there is no killer or one who causes killing, no hearer or one who causes hearing, no cognizer or one who causes cognition.
Even when one cuts off another's head with a sharp sword, no one deprives anyone of life;
rather, the sword merely passes through the opening between the seven bodies.
Furthermore, there are these fourteen hundred thousand principal wombs, along with sixty-six hundred [secondary ones].
five hundred and five types of action, three types of action, action and half-action,
the sixty-two paths of practice, the sixty-two intermediate eons, the six classes of birth, the eight stages of a person,
forty-nine hundred modes of livelihood, forty-nine hundred types of wanderers, forty-nine hundred abodes of nāgas, twenty hundred faculties, thirty...
One hundred hells, thirty-six realms of dust, seven wombs of perception, seven wombs of non-perception, seven wombs of wriggling,
seven classes of gods, seven classes of humans, seven classes of *pesācas*, seven lakes, seven whirlpools,
seven precipices, seven hundred precipices, seven dreams, seven hundred dreams, and eighty-four thousand great eons (*mahākappa*).

"Whatever [beings], whether fools or wise, having run on and wandered through the cycle of existence, will make an end of suffering—therein it is not the case that 'by this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall ripen unripened karma, or by repeatedly experiencing ripened karma, I shall bring it to an end. For thus there is no such thing;
pleasure and pain are measured out like a bushel, the cycle of existence is limited, and there is no decrease or increase, no rising up or falling down."
"Just as a ball of thread, when thrown, unwinds only until it is exhausted, even so,
after wandering and transmigrating, both the fool and the wise will make an end of suffering.
In this regard, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus:
“This teacher, sir, speaks thus and holds this view:
‘There are these seven bodies that are unmade, not produced by a maker, uncreated, not created by a creator, barren, stable as a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar.
They do not move, they do not change, and they do not obstruct one another.’”
They are not capable of bringing about each other’s pleasure, or pain, or both pleasure and pain.
Which seven?
The earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, pleasure, pain, and the living being as the seventh.
These seven bodies are unmade, not fashioned by a maker, uncreated, not created by a creator, barren, fixed like a mountain peak, standing firm like a pillar.
They do not move, they do not change, and they do not obstruct one another.
They are incapable of bringing about either the pleasure or the pain, or both the pleasure and the pain, of one another.
In this regard, there is no killer nor one who causes killing, no hearer nor one who causes hearing, no cognizer nor one who causes cognition.
Even when someone cuts off a head with a sharp sword, no one deprives anyone of life;
rather, the sword merely passes through the opening between the seven bodies.
Now, there are these fourteen hundred thousand principal wombs,
sixty-six hundred, five hundred actions, five actions, three actions, action and half-action, sixty-two paths,
sixty-two intermediate aeons, six classes of rebirth, eight stages of manhood, and four hundred and ninety-nine modes of livelihood.
Forty-nine hundred wandering ascetics, forty-nine hundred abodes of nāgas, twenty hundred faculties, thirty hundred hells,
thirty-six realms of dust, seven wombs of percipient beings, seven wombs of non-percipient beings, seven wombs of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient beings,
seven gods, seven humans, seven petas, seven lakes, seven whirlpools, seven precipices, and seven...
Hundreds of falls, seven dreams, seven hundred dreams, and eighty-four thousand great aeons—
having run on and wandered through these, both fools and the wise will make an end of suffering. In this regard,
there is nothing [to be gained] by means of this morality, or vow, or austerity, or holy life that is yet unripened.
"Or, 'I shall bring my karma to fruition,' or 'Having encountered matured karma, I shall exhaust it as it arises'—it is not so.
Pleasure and pain are measured like a grain-measure; saṃsāra is limited; there is no decrease or increase, no waxing or waning.
Just as when a ball of thread is thrown, it unwinds only until it is completely spent."
"In the very same way, both the fool and the wise, having run on and wandered through the cycle of existence, will make an end of suffering.
But if the word of this venerable teacher is true, then what I have not done here has been done by me; what I have not lived out here has been lived out by me.
We are both equal and alike here, having attained the state of a recluse—just as I do not say, "Both of us, having run on and wandered through the cycle of existence, shall make an end of suffering."
Yet this nakedness, this shaven head, this crouching exertion, and this plucking out of hair and beard of our venerable teacher are excessive;
for while I dwell in a bed crowded with children, enjoy Kāsī sandalwood, wear garlands, scents, and ointments,
and accept gold and silver, I shall have the same destination as this venerable teacher in the life hereafter.
Knowing what and seeing what should I practice the holy life under this teacher? Thinking,
“This is an unholylife,” he becomes disillusioned with that holy life and departs.
This, Sandaka, is the fourth dwelling in the non-holy life proclaimed by that Blessed One— who knows and sees, who is an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha—
wherein a wise person would not dwell even for a moment in the holy life,
and while dwelling there, would not achieve the method, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.
"These, Sandaka, are the four ways of living the non-holy life that have been declared by that Blessed One— who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
wherein a wise person would not live the holy life with confidence,
and while living there, would not attain the method, the Dhamma, and what is wholesome."
“It is wonderful, Master Ānanda! It is marvelous, Master Ānanda!

To what extent the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—has declared four things that are not a life of the holy life to be ‘not a life of the holy life,’ wherein a wise person would not, even with difficulty, live the holy life...”
He might dwell there, yet while dwelling there, he would not attain the true way,

the Dhamma, and what is wholesome. But what, Master Ānanda, are those four non-consoling spiritual lives (brahmacariya) that have been declared by the Blessed One— the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
wherein a wise person, even with difficulty, [would find no consolation]?
“Would one not live there, and while living there, would one not fail to realize the method, the Dhamma, and what is wholesome?
“In this case, Sandaka, a certain teacher claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, to possess knowledge and vision without remainder, declaring:
‘Whether I am walking or standing, asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously present to me.’”
Thus he enters even an empty house; he does not receive alms; a cock bites him;
he encounters a fierce elephant, he encounters a fierce horse, he encounters a fierce bull;
he asks for the name and clan of women and men; and he asks for the name of a village or town, or for the way.
Thus, when asked, "What was this?", he replied: "It was necessary for me to enter an empty house;
therefore I entered it. It was necessary that I receive no alms; therefore I received none. It was necessary that I be bitten by a dog; therefore I was bitten.
It was necessary that I encounter a fierce elephant; therefore I encountered one. It was necessary that I encounter a fierce horse..."
‘It was necessary that I should encounter a fierce bull,’ so I encountered it;
‘It was necessary that I should ask both the woman’s and the man’s name and clan,’ so I asked;
‘It was necessary that I should ask the name of the village or town and the way,’ so I asked.
In this regard, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus:

“This venerable teacher claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, possessing knowledge and vision without remainder... [as before] ...he even had to ask for the name of a village, a town, a road, or a direction; therefore he asked.
He concludes: “This holy life is not inspiring confidence.”
Having understood this, one becomes disillusioned with that holy life and departs from it.
This, Sandaka, is the first uninspiring holy life proclaimed by the Blessed One— the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One,
the Perfectly Enlightened One— in which a wise person would not, even with difficulty, live the holy life.
He might dwell there, yet while dwelling there, he would not master the method, the Dhamma, and what is wholesome.
Furthermore, Sandaka, here a certain teacher is one who relies on oral tradition, one whose doctrine is based on oral tradition.
He teaches the Dhamma by means of oral tradition, based on "thus it was said" and "thus it was handed down," through the transmission of the scriptural collections.

But for a teacher who relies on oral tradition, Sandaka, whose truth is based on oral tradition, there is what has been well-heard and what has been poorly heard; there is what is so and what is otherwise.
In this regard, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus:

"This venerable teacher is one who relies on oral tradition, whose truth is based on oral tradition; he teaches the Dhamma by means of oral tradition, by way of 'so it has been said,' through successive tradition, and through the mastery of the Pitakas."

But in the case of a teacher who relies on oral tradition and whose truth is based on oral tradition, there is what has been well-heard and what has been poorly heard; there is what is so and what is otherwise.
Having understood, "This holy life is not a source of consolation," he becomes disillusioned with that holy life and departs from it.
This, Sandaka, is the second uninspiring holy life proclaimed by that Blessed One— who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
wherein a wise person would not live the holy life with confidence,
and while living it, would not attain the method, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.
Furthermore, Sandaka, here a certain teacher is a reasoner and an investigator.
He teaches a Dhamma that is hammered out by reasoning, followed by investigation, and derived from his own inspiration.
Now, for such a teacher who is a reasoner and an investigator, what he has well-reasoned may turn out to be ill-reasoned; what he has reasoned correctly may turn out to be otherwise.
In this regard, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus:
‘This venerable teacher is a reasoner and an investigator.
He teaches a Dhamma that is hammered out by reasoning, followed by investigation, and derived from his own inspired insight.’
But as for the teacher Takki, who relies on investigation, his teaching is sometimes well-reasoned and sometimes poorly reasoned; it is sometimes so and sometimes otherwise.
Having understood, "This holy life does not provide consolation," he becomes disillusioned with that holy life and departs from it.
This, Sandaka, is the third uninspiring holy life proclaimed by that Blessed One— who knows and sees, who is an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha—
wherein a wise person would not live the holy life with confidence,
and while living it, would not achieve the method, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.
Furthermore, Sandaka, here some teacher is dull and bewildered.
Because of his dullness and bewilderment, when questioned on various points, he resorts to verbal evasion and to theeel-wriggling of the Eel-Wriggler (*amarāvikkhepa*), saying:
"It is so for me, it is not so for me, it is otherwise for me, it is not for me, it is not not for me."
In this regard, Sandaka, a wise person reflects thus:
‘This venerable teacher is dull and deluded.
Because of his dullness and delusion, when questioned on various points, he resorts to verbal wriggling and to the equivocation of an endless debate.’
‘It is not thus for me,’ ‘It is so for me,’ ‘It is otherwise for me,’ ‘It is not for me,’ ‘It is not not for me’—
knowing, “This holy life is without consolation,” he becomes disillusioned with that holy life and departs.
This, Sandaka, is the fourth uninspiring holy life proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
wherein a wise person would not live the holy life with confidence,
nor, while living it, would he attain the method, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.
"These, Sandaka, are those four non-consoling holy lives proclaimed by that Blessed One— who knows and sees, who is an Arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha—
wherein a wise person would not live the holy life even with difficulty,
and while living there, would not attain the true Dhamma and the wholesome."
“It is wonderful, Master Ānanda! It is marvelous, Master Ānanda!

To what an extent the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—has declared these four non-conducive holy lives to be ‘non-conducive holy lives,’ wherein a wise person would not venture to live the holy life.”

“One might not live the holy life, or if one were to live it, one might not attain the method, the Dhamma that is wholesome. But what, Master Ānanda, is the doctrine of that Teacher, what does he proclaim, wherein a wise person may live the holy life with its possibilities, and while living it, may attain the method, the Dhamma that is wholesome? “In this case, Sandaka, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, perfectly enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. …” [as above] … “He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. [as above] … “That is the doctrine of that Teacher, that is what he proclaims, wherein a wise person may live the holy life with its possibilities, and while living it, may attain the method, the Dhamma that is wholesome. [as above] … “Therefore, Sandaka, if you wish, go to that Teacher and approach him. [as above] … “I will do so, Master Ānanda. [as above] … “Then, Sandaka, if you wish, go to that Teacher and approach him. [as above] … “I will do so, Master Ānanda. [as above] … “Then, Sandaka, if you wish, go to that Teacher and approach him. [as above] … “I will do so, Master Ānanda. [as above] … “Then, Sandaka, if you wish, go to that Teacher and approach him. [as above] … “I will do so, Master Ānanda. [as above] … “Then, Sandaka, if you wish, go to that Teacher and approach him. [as above] … “I will do so, Master Ānanda. [as above] … “Then, Sandaka, if you wish, go to that Teacher and approach him. [as above] … “I will do so, Master Ānanda. [as above] … “Then, Sandaka, if you wish, go to that Teacher and approach him. [as above] … “I will do so, Master Ānanda. [as above] … “Then, Sandaka, if you wish, go to that Teacher and approach him. [as above] … “I will do so, Master Ānanda. [as above] … “Then, Sandaka, if you wish, go to that Teacher and approach him. [as above] … “I will do so, Master Ānanda. [as above] … “Then, Sandaka, if you wish, go to that Teacher and approach him. [as above] … “I will do so, Master Ānanda. Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—he, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

Sandaka, when a disciple attains such a sublime distinction under a teacher, a wise person would live the holy life under him as long as possible; and while living there, he would succeed in the way, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.
Furthermore, Sandaka, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna...

[as above]... Furthermore, Sandaka, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells in equanimity... [as above]... and enters and dwells in the third jhāna. In whatever teacher’s dispensation a disciple attains such a sublime distinction, there a wise person would live the holy life with diligence; and while living there, he would succeed in the way, in the Dhamma, and in what is wholesome.

"Sandaka, when a disciple attains such a sublime distinction under a teacher, a wise person would live the holy life there with diligence; and living there, he would succeed in the way that is noble, the Dhamma that is wholesome.
Furthermore, Sandaka, by the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna."

Sandaka, when a disciple attains such a sublime distinction under a teacher, a wise person would live the holy life there with diligence; and while living there, he would succeed in the way that is reasonable, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.

With his mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
Thus he recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births... [as far as] thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.

Sandaka, when a disciple attains such a sublime distinction under a teacher, a wise person would live the holy life there under him with diligence; and while living there, he would succeed in the way, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

Sandaka, when a disciple attains such a sublime distinction under a teacher, a wise person would live the holy life there with diligence; and while living there, he would succeed in the method, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.

With his mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
Thus he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; he understands as it really is:
"This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
One understands as it really is: "These are the taints"; one understands as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints";
one understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of the taints"; one understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints."

For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: "It is liberated.
One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."

“Sandaka, when a disciple attains such a sublime distinction under a Teacher, a wise person would live the holy life there with diligence; and while living there, he would succeed in the methodical Dhamma that is wholesome.

“But, Master Ānanda, would that bhikkhu—an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge—would he enjoy sensual pleasures?”

“Sandaka, that bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is incapable of transgressing in five respects.
A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life;
a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of taking what is not given, which is called theft; a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse.”

A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of speaking a deliberate lie; a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures by means of hoarding, just as he did formerly when he was a householder.
Sandaka, that bhikkhu who is an arahant with taints destroyed, one who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal...
“One who has utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, who is liberated through right knowledge— he is incapable of transgressing these five points.
“But as for that bhikkhu, Master Ānanda, who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done,
laid down the burden, attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed, and who is liberated through right knowledge— whether he is walking or standing...”
“Is knowledge and vision constantly and continuously established in you, whether you are asleep or awake:
‘My taints are exhausted’?
“In that case, Sandaka, I will give you a simile.”
By means of a simile, Sandaka, some wise people understand the meaning of what is said.
It is just as if a man’s hands and feet were cut off;
whether he is walking, standing, asleep, or awake, he constantly and continuously knows [his state].
“Does that man know, while constantly and continuously reflecting, ‘My hands and feet have been cut off,’ or does he know it only when he reflects upon it? “No,
Master Ānanda, that man does not know it constantly and continuously.”
‘My hands and feet have been cut off.
Nevertheless, when he reflects upon it, he knows:
‘My hands and feet have been cut off.’”
“In the same way, Sandaka, for that bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done,
laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—
whether he is walking or standing, asleep or awake— knowledge and vision are not constantly and continuously present before him:”
‘My taints are exhausted’;
moreover, when he reflects upon them, he knows:
‘My taints are exhausted.’”
“But how many, Master Ānanda, are there who have reached liberation in this Dhamma and Discipline?

“Not just one hundred, Sandaka, nor two hundred, nor three hundred, nor four hundred, nor five hundred; rather, there are even more than that who have reached liberation in this Dhamma and Discipline.
“It is wonderful, Master Ānanda! It is marvelous, Master Ānanda!”

"There will indeed be no exalting of one's own doctrine nor disparaging of the doctrines of others, and there will be teaching of the Dhamma in its proper sphere, and many who have attained deliverance will be seen.
But these Ājīvakas—who are like sons whose mother has died—exalt themselves and disparage others, and they proclaim only three deliverers, namely:
Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla."
Then the wanderer Sandaka addressed his own assembly:
"Gentlemen, practice the holy life under the ascetic Gotama.
It is no longer easy for us to renounce gain, honor, and fame."
Thus did the wanderer Sandaka dismiss his own assembly from the Blessed One’s holy life.
The Sandaka Sutta, the sixth, is finished.
